Data were excluded from the analyses in cases where a sample was physically lost (i.e., because a cell pellet was aspirated or the cell sorter encountered a technical issue) and/or RT-qPCR replicates where there was no amplification or where housekeeping gene Ct values were substantially different than all other samples. The experiments were not randomized. The Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments and outcome assessment.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Schuyler and colleagues explored the feasibility of expanding epigenome editing with newly created
dCas12a-based epigenome editors. They thoroughly tested previously described dCas12a systems with various
improvements and benchmarked the editing efficiency at a wide range of target genes and different cell lines. Notably, the
authors leveraged Pol II-driven pre-crRNA transcription to expand usable crRNA usage due to the processivity of Pol II and
the dCas12a’s ability to cleave and load the final cRNAs. Leveraging the fact that AsCas12a and LbCas12a utilize different
PAM sequences to find their target in the genome, the authors built a simultaneously activating and repressing system
where the various versions of Cas12a cleverly facilitate the opposite role of gene regulation.
On a personal note, I would like to thank the authors for a beautifully written and well-edited manuscript, which was an
absolute pleasure to read – something that is unfortunately rare these days. Much thought went into the clarity of the figures
and the accompanying manuscript text.
Minor points:
- Figures with box plots: Plotting the individual dots for each measurement would benefit from added jitter to identify each dot
and prevent overplotting. This will enable viewers to see if there were dropouts (n=2 instead of n=3)
- Figure 1 c -e: the use of red for the front and back cRNAs, the HBE1 gene, and the CAG promoter is very confusing. This
figure would benefit from consistency in color choice. For example, Fig 1c could have 4 constructs shown with U6 and CAG
separated, and the color would then be used in Fig 1d and 1e again.
- Also, since some people might be color blind, the color for AS and LB in Figures 1a and 1b might be problematic
- The main text could explain the choice of crRNA sequences or reference previously established sequences.
- In Figure 2 f-g, which demonstrates multiplexed repression of multiple target genes - the 4xSID fusion represses slightly
better than the KRAB fusion. This is compared to figures 2c and 2d, where it appears to be the other way around for
RAB11A. Are the targeting crRNAs for RAB11A and VEGFA identical across Figures 2c-d and 2f-g? Does the positioning or
the multiplexing of the target crRNAs for Fig 2f-g attribute to differences in repression?
- Fig 2 e-g: The authors chose to measure repression of RNA after 48h. Since repression of RNA is also dependent on RNA
stability and KRAB vs Sin3A repression might have different dynamics, a time point at 72h or 96h post-transduction would
help to understand if the repressive strength is time-dependent or not.
- Figure 4: It would be helpful to have the statistical analysis depicted right in the figure (e.g. lines indicating the samples
compared and asterisk for levels of significance)
- Figure 4: Labeling the target genes above the panels and not only using color to denote target genes helps clarity
- In addition, to help the reader judge fold activation and repression, please add TPM (transcript per million from gene
expression data sets) for each target gene next to the gene label. 3,200-fold activation is likely only possible on non-
expressed genes vs 2-fold activation on a different target gene.
- Figure 5: The two Cas12a orthologues have been shown to confer different transcriptional effects. Did the authors also test
using dHyperLbCas12a for activation and dEnAsCas12a for repression?
- No comment or experiment has been performed to address the stability of the epigenome edits. While I wouldn’t expect this
to be done for every cell and target gene presented, it would be interesting to know how quickly the enhancers of PER1 will
be reset after targeted repression, for example.
- Figure 7 and the experiment screening crRNAs to repress PER1 enhancers: The analysis of which crRNAs were most
effective at promoting enhancer silencing was not performed. It would be beneficial for the reader to understand if there are
any rules or considerations for crRNA positioning relative to CREs.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In the current manuscript, Melore et al. has combined dHyperLbCas12a with RNA Polymerase II expression of long crRNA for efficient highly-multiplexed epigenome editing. The authors have demonstrated that dHyperLbCas12a is compatible with different activation and repression domains. The authors further showed that this system can perform simultaneous activation and repression using a single crRNA array, and is effective for high-throught screens. Based on these, the authors use dHyperLbCas12a-KRAB and a barcoded library of crRNA arrays for dissecting the cis-regulatory architecture for a dose-dependent gene expression response to glucocorticoids.
Overall, the study is interesting and the findings are useful to the multiplexed gene expression regulation subfield. However, the study is minimal on its novelty in terms of the methods it employed. The novelty and importance of dCas12a mediated the multiplexed activation and repression have been well-demonstrated already in previous publication. Perhaps, the authors can expand on some other high-throughput screening applications and . In addtion, some data are robust and not enough. Here are some comments and suggestions for the authors to improve the quality of the work.
1.The authors state that they optimized the dCas12a epigenome editing system, but both the Cas protein and the regulatory elements have been reported before. Explain why chose these Cas12a variants, and not other variants or even other family such as Cas12i. And the statement that dHyperLbCas12a and dEnAsCas12a outperform the wild type dCas12a variants for epigenome editing, has been already reported. In addition, it is recommended to add more sites to compare the activity of encas12a and hypercas12a.
2.It’s reported that RNA Pol II promoter CAG could improve the dCas12a pre-crRNA expression of long arrays, such as over 40 crRNAs. Explain or supplement experimental evidence for why CAG was chosen over other RNA Pol II promoters.
3.Explain why chose the transcriptional regulatory elements VPR, P300, KRAB and 4xSID, not other such as SAM, Tet et al. It would be helpful to include more context on how this system compares to other multiplexed gene editing techniques, such as multiplexed CRISPRa or CRISPRi, particularly in terms of efficiency, cost, and ease of implementation.
4.The data showed that dCas12a-VPR is significantly better than dCas12a-P300, but the author stated that dCas12a-P300 fusions robustly activate gene expression. Please explain this. The authors should add more sites to compare the activity of dCas12a-P300 and dCas12a-VPR when targeting a gene enhancer and/or promoter.
5.Provide more detail on the hybrid pre-crRNA array strategy for simultaneous activation and repression, such as fornt or back combination of crRNA for activation and repression. Include a discussion on whether this approach could be extended to other types of dCas effectors, such as those for DNA methylation or histone modification.
6.Expand the discussion on potential off-target effects, particularly when using multiplexed crRNA arrays. Although only at the cellular level of high throughput screening, include experiments or simulations that demonstrate the safety of the system in minimizing off-target interactions.
7.In the figures section, appropriate statistical analysis should be conducted, and p-value indicated to assess the authors’ claim.
8.The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed description of the statistical methods used to analyze gene expression changes, particularly in high-throughput screens. Specify how multiple hypothesis testing was corrected and how significant results were defined.
9.In general, the biological replicates are 3 or over. Thus, it is recommended that for activity comparison of among these variants, while many group in this article only one set. This is not rigorous.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript presents the development and characterization of dCas12a-based gene silencing and activation using two distinct dCas12a variants. The authors employed enhanced versions of dCas12a, enAsCas12a and HyperLbCas12a, along with crRNA arrays to modulate gene expression. They demonstrate that dCas12a can be coupled with the activation domain P300 and the repression domain SID. They show simultaneous activation and repression of target genes through a single crRNA array by co-expressing both enAsCas12a and HyperLbCas12a. Furthermore, they illustrate the platform's utility in screening applications using a barcoded library of crRNA arrays targeting two enhancers of a single gene.
Overall, the study offers a side-by-side comparison of gene activation and repression across two different Cas12a systems. It provides a resource for using AsCas12a and LbCas12a variants in gene regulation. For example, the observation that dLbCas12a-P300 fusions exhibit stronger and more consistent activation than dAsCas12a-P300 fusions is interesting.
While the fusion of Cas12a to P300 and SID is new, these tools do not outperform established systems such as VPR for activation and KRAB for repression.
However, the manuscript raises major concerns that should be addressed before it can be considered for publication:
1. The potential for crosstalk between the two Cas12a variants should be thoroughly evaluated. Both variants utilize the same PAM and share similar guide RNA structures. This raises concerns about their orthogonality. To confirm their suitability for simultaneous activation and repression, the authors should demonstrate that each Cas12a does not interact with the other's guide RNA. Additional experimental data are required to validate their orthogonality and crosstalk.
2. The title, "Highly multiplexed epigenome editing screens," is misleading and overstates the study's scope. The manuscript demonstrates the activation of four genes, and it remains unconvincing that all four genes are all activated in single cells. This falls short compared to prior studies that activated or repressed a greater number of genes. Additionally, the term "epigenome editing" is not fully substantiated, as the authors only present transcription-level activation or repression without characterizing epigenetic modifications. Moreover, the screens are limited to targeting two enhancers, which does not align with the claim of high multiplexing. The title should be revised to accurately reflect the data presented in the study.
3. It is unclear how most data were collected. For example, how was flow cytometry gating defined? How many replicates were performed? How many biological or technical replicates were tested in each experimental group? Additionally, statistics are lacking in the figures, and p-values should be included.
4. Although the authors tested a few cell lines for characterization, the study would have greater utility if additional cell types, particularly primary cells, were included. This would enhance the relevance and applicability of the findings for the community.
5. The inclusion of a control library with 10,000 non-targeting six-crRNA arrays and three pre-crRNAs targeting the PER1 promoter seems excessive. The rationale for this large imbalance between non-targeting and targeting arrays should be clarified. How does this control design contribute to the study's objectives?
6. The diagrams in Fig. 7b-d are confusing. Are these plots representing PER1-high cells or PER1-low cells? A more detailed explanation of how these plots were generated is necessary to help understanding.
7. The purpose of testing the two enhancers using a large library is unclear. The authors should elaborate on why not use a few well-designed crRNA arrays to target individual or paired enhancers and measure the downstream gene expression? It is unclear if there is a necessity of performing library screening on two enhancers of one gene. Furthermore, the insights gained from testing PER1 enhancers can be strengthened.
8. The manuscript would benefit from discussing specific design rules for guide RNA arrays.
9. Citations 73-74: The manuscript does not appropriately cite work on Cas13. The authors should ensure they reference the most relevant studies.

Reviewer #4:
This manuscript presents the development and characterization of dCas12a-based gene silencing
and activation using two distinct dCas12a variants. The authors employed enhanced versions of
dCas12a, enAsCas12a and HyperLbCas12a, along with crRNA arrays to modulate gene expression.
They demonstrate that dCas12a can be coupled with the activation domain P300 and the repression
domain SID. They show simultaneous activation and repression of target genes through a single
crRNA array by co-expressing both enAsCas12a and HyperLbCas12a. Furthermore, they illustrate
the platform's utility in screening applications using a barcoded library of crRNA arrays targeting two
enhancers of a single gene.
Overall, the study offers a side-by-side comparison of gene activation and repression across two
different Cas12a systems. It provides a resource for using AsCas12a and LbCas12a variants in gene
regulation. For example, the observation that dLbCas12a-P300 fusions exhibit stronger and more
consistent activation than dAsCas12a-P300 fusions is interesting. While the fusion of Cas12a to P300
and SID is new, these tools do not outperform established systems such as VPR for activation and
KRAB for repression.
However, the manuscript raises major concerns that should be addressed before it can be considered
for publication:
1. The potential for crosstalk between the two Cas12a variants should be thoroughly evaluated. Both
variants utilize the same PAM and share similar guide RNA structures. This raises concerns about
their orthogonality. To confirm their suitability for simultaneous activation and repression, the authors
should demonstrate that each Cas12a does not interact with the other's guide RNA. Additional
experimental data are required to validate their orthogonality and crosstalk.

I commend the authors for incorporating targeted gene activation in primary cells, which adds significant value beyond standard cell line models. Their acknowledgment of the differences in performance compared to HEK293T cells provides important perspective. I also appreciate the authors’ transparency in noting that not all target genes respond equally to activation—an important consideration for future studies, particularly those with therapeutic aims.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
“The data showed that dCas12a-VPR is significantly better than dCas12a-P300, but the author stated that dCas12a-P300 fusions robustly activate gene expression. Please explain this. The authors should add more sites to compare the activity of dCas12a-P300 and dCas12a-VPR when targeting a gene enhancer and/or promoter.”
Regarding this question, the authors did not provide a reasonable response. The authors state that "dCas12a-P300 fusions robustly activate gene expression", but this conclusion cannot be drawn from their data, which instead shows that dCas12a-VPR has higher activity. Moreover, while the authors claim dCas12a-P300 is more suitable for gene activation expression from distal regulatory elements, the data indicates that dCas12a-VPR exhibits higher activity targeting MYOD1 distal regulatory region (DRR). The authors need to clarify the purpose of comparing the activity between enAsCas12a and LbCas12a, not dhyperCas12a in the Supp Fig. 3c-f. Similarly, the statement "dCas12a-P300 fusions enable multiplexed gene activation in human cell lines" is problematic. We recommend the authors revise the title and provide clearer descriptions.
The authors have appropriately supplemented the data or reasonably addressed other comments.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This revised manuscript introduces the simultaneous regulation of multiple genes, by expressing crRNA arrays from an RNA polymerase II promoter, using engineered dCas12a variants, dHyperLbCas12a and dEnAsCas12a. In addition to activation domain VPR and repression domain KRAB, they demonstrated that dCas12a can be coupled with activation domain P300 and repression domain 4xSID. They showed the platform’s capability with multiple cell lines: cancer cell lines, human T cells, and iPSCs. They further validate their approach in two screenings: a low MOI fitness screen and an enhancer screen that assessed dose-dependent control of PER1 by two glucocorticoid-responsive enhancers. This side-by-side comparison of dHyperLbCas12a-KRAB, dHyperLbCas12a-4xSID, dEnAsCas12a-KRAB, and dEnAsCas12a-4xSID in low MOI fitness screen illustrated that dHyperLbCas12a-KRAB carries stronger activity. While the revision represents a clear improvement over the prior submission, several issues remain and should be addressed before the work is considered for publication.
Major comments:
1. In Figure 2, authors show data for the simultaneous repression of 4 genes in HEK cells and 5 genes in primary T cells. However, in primary T cells, repression is not statistically significant across all target genes and donors. This suggests that multiplex repression is cell-type dependent, which is a limitation to their screening application. This cell-type dependent and gene-dependent performance should be acknowledged in the text.
2. This sentence is ambiguous: "While we do not observe effects for all target genes in this cell type, these results indicate the potential of using dCas12a for multiplexed repression in primary cells." The authors should clarify and revise this text.
3. Authors showed activation of core and accessory neuronal differentiation genes can induce moderate expression of TUBB3. However, what is the benefit or advantage of using this system for cell differentiation? TUBB3 is an early marker for differentiation; it doesn’t indicate full neuronal identity.
4. Improving the visualization in Figure 8 to more clearly distinguish between enhancer level and shift would help convey the message more effectively. For example, adding a bar indicating the mean value for each group and statistical tests.
5. What has been learned from their enhancer screening? The manuscript would benefit from biological insights learned from their screening.
6. In their qPCR method, it is important to clarify how many technical replicates were performed.
7. P-values are noted in the caption of Figure 2. The authors didn't label any P-values in the figures. In Figure 1, there is no statistical comparison between the control and experimental groups.
8. The authors should include clear explanation why in Fig. 4g “Core+Accessory” shows similar or slightly weaker mCherry+ cells% compared to “NGN3”, but in Fig. 4h mCherry MFI is higher for “Core+Accessory”. This is a discrepancy that should be explained.
9. The authors should pay close attention to statistics and clearly label them in the figure or caption. Raw flow cytometry and qPCR data and screening results should be made publicly available.
Minor comments:
1. The way authors labeled supplementary data is inconsistent. Some are Supp Fig xx, some are Supp. Fig xx and Supplementary Fig. xx.
2. In Figure 4, does dHyperLbCas12a-P300 work in primary T cells?
3. The title said “HyperCas12a enables multiplexed CRISPRi screens”, but to be precise, they used HyperdCas12a, the catalytically dead version.
4. Fig S6g-h: the figure legend or the figure itself should clearly state which crRNA these diagrams use.
5. Line 486: duplicate words

response to glucocorticoids.

subfield. However, the study is minimal on its novelty in terms of the methods it employed. The novelty and
importance of dCas12a mediated the multiplexed activation and repression have been well-demonstrated
already in previous publication. Perhaps, the authors can expand on some other high-throughput screening

suggestions for the authors to improve the quality of the work.

enhancers of a single gene.
Overall, the study offers a side-by-side comparison of gene activation and repression across two
different Cas12a systems. It provides a resource for using AsCas12a and LbCas12a variants in gene
regulation. For example, the observation that dLbCas12a-P300 fusions exhibit stronger and more
consistent activation than dAsCas12a-P300 fusions is interesting. While the fusion of Cas12a to P300
and SID is new, these tools do not outperform established systems such as VPR for activation and
KRAB for repression.
However, the manuscript raises major concerns that should be addressed before it can be considered
for publication:
1. The potential for crosstalk between the two Cas12a variants should be thoroughly evaluated. Both
variants utilize the same PAM and share similar guide RNA structures. This raises concerns about
their orthogonality. To confirm their suitability for simultaneous activation and repression, the authors
should demonstrate that each Cas12a does not interact with the other's guide RNA. Additional
experimental data are required to validate their orthogonality and crosstalk.
Thank you for this comment, we have performed additional experiments to address these concerns.
The data is shown in Supp. Fig. 6g-h and the text on lines 510-531 describing them reads:
To evaluate crosstalk in such a setting, we co-transfected dHyperLbCas12a-VPR with
the hybrid pre-crRNA containing AsCas12a crRNAs for activation as well as either
dEnAsCas12a or Cas9 as a transfection control for number and size of plasmids. We
found that, by itself, dHyperLbCas12a-VPR can use AsCas12a crRNAs but with less
efficacy than homologous LbCas12a crRNAs. Specifically, when dHyperLbCas12a-VPR
was cotransfected with Cas9, there was 150-fold activation of HBE1 and no significant
activation of MYOD1 (Supp. Fig 6g). The observed activation of HBE1 was ~30-fold
less than when dHyperLbCas12a-VPR was co-transfected with its homologous hybrid
pre-crRNA array (Supp. Fig 6a).
However, that crosstalk is alleviated when dHyperLbCas12a and dEnAsCas12a are both
present and competing for crRNAs. Specifically, when dHyperLbCas12a-VPR was
co-transfected with dEnAsCas12a, we observed no significant activation of either gene,
and relative HBE1 expression dropped to a 1.25-fold change over non-targeting control
(Supp. Fig 6g).
That result was essentially similar when we tested dEnAsCas12a-VPR in the same way.
Specifically, dEnAsCas12a-VPR was able to significantly activate HBE1 by ~6.5 fold
using LbCas12a crRNAs when co-transfected with Cas9. However, there was no effect
when dEnAsCas12a-VPR was co-transfected with dHyperLbCas12a (Supp. Fig 6h).
Together, these results confirm that while dEnAsCas12a and dHyperLbCas12a cannorthologous crRNAs for activation, they are not able to do so when the homologous
Cas12a is also present and competing for crRNAs, such as in the hybrid pre-crRNA
system developed here.
2. The title, "Highly multiplexed epigenome editing screens," is misleading and overstates the study's
scope. The manuscript demonstrates the activation of four genes, and it remains unconvincing that all
four genes are all activated in single cells. This falls short compared to prior studies that activated or
repressed a greater number of genes. Additionally, the term "epigenome editing" is not fully
substantiated, as the authors only present transcription-level activation or repression without
characterizing epigenetic modifications. Moreover, the screens are limited to targeting two enhancers,
which does not align with the claim of high multiplexing. The title should be revised to accurately
reflect the data presented in the study.
Thank you for this comment, we have revised the title to “HyperCas12a enables multiplexed CRISPRi
screens”, which we believe better reflects the scope of the study.
3. It is unclear how most data were collected. For example, how was flow cytometry gating defined?
How many replicates were performed? How many biological or technical replicates were tested in
each experimental group? Additionally, statistics are lacking in the figures, and p-values should be
included.
Flow cytometry gating is described in the methods and now shown in Supp. Figs 5, 16, and 18.
Biological replicates are described in figure legends and p values are described in the text, and we
have now added asterisks to Fig. 2-7 and Supp. Figs 1, 2, 4, 6, and 10 to denote significance where
appropriate. We also increased jitter in Fig. 2-7 so that the number of replicates can be more clearly
seen in the figures. A full summary of statistical tests performed is available in Supp. Table 1.
4. Although the authors tested a few cell lines for characterization, the study would have
greater utility if additional cell types, particularly primary cells, were included. This would
enhance the relevance and applicability of the findings for the community.
Thank you for this comment. Addressing this comment was one of the major focuses of our revised
manuscript. We performed numerous additional experiments to address these concerns. We tested
the effects of stably expressed dCas12a effectors and pre-crRNA arrays in primary human T Cells
and iPSCs. The results of these experiments are displayed in Fig. 2h-j and Fig. 4e-h. The text related
to the T cell repression results in on line 284-292 and reads:
Next, we co-transduced human T cells from three independent donors with
dHyperLbCas12a-KRAB or dEnAsCas12a-KRAB and either a pre-crRNA targeting the
promoters of SLA2, GATA3, MAP4K1, GRAP, and LAT2 or a control pre-crRNA
containing ten non-targeting crRNAs (Fig. 2h). We observe similar trends for both
Cas12a orthologues. For example, both dEnAsCas12a- and dHyperLbCas12a-KRAB
showed the strongest repression of GRAP and LAT2, though dHyperLbCas12a showed
stronger repression (mean log fold change across donors of -0.89 and -0.87 vs. -0.47
2
and -0.42) consistent with our previous findings (Fig. 2i-j). While we do not observe
effects for all target genes in this cell type, these results indicate the potential of using
dCas12a for multiplexed repression in primary cells.
The text related to activation experiments in T Cells and iPSCs reads is on lines 397-440 and reads:
Model systems for studying primary cell differentiation commonly involve controlling the
expression of several genes at once16,69. As a key step towards such highly multiplexed
control of gene regulation in primary cells, we focused on demonstrating dCas12a-based
gene activation in T cells and in an human induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-based
model of neuronal differentiation.
To demonstrate multiplexed control of gene expression in T cells, we co-transduced
dHyperLbCas12a-VPR along with the pre-crRNA targeting AR, HBE1 and MYOD1 into
primary human CD3+ T cells from three different donors. The results were similar to
those observed in cell lines, namely that there was significant activation (p < 0.05,
One-Sided Student's Paired T-Test) of HBE1 and MYOD1, with effects ranging from
~45-350-fold upregulation (Fig.4e). Also as in the cell lines, there was little or no
activation of AR gene expression.
To demonstrate multiplexed control of gene expression in iPSC cell differentiation, we
used an iPSC cell line that had previously been modified to express mCherry
cotranslationally with TUBB3A, a marker of neuronal differentiation13. We further
modified the line to stably express dHyperLbCas12a-VPR. We designed a pre-crRNA
array of three crRNAs to target the promoter of NGN3, a strong driver of neuronal
differentiation, to act as a positive control. We also designed a pre-crRNA array
containing seven crRNAs that target three core neurogenic transcription factors (deemed
“Core”): NGN1, NGN2, and NGN3. We designed a pre-crRNA array containing seven
crRNAs that target four accessory genes that have been shown to enhance neuronal
differentiation when co-activated in tandem with a core factor (deemed “Accessory”):
LHX6, LHX8, SOX2, and E2F713. Lastly, we designed a pre-crRNA array containing all
14 crRNAs and targeting both core and accessory factors together (deemed
“Core+Accessory”) (Fig. 4f).
We transduced the dHyperLbCas12a-VPR cell line with these pre-crRNAs and then
measured the percentage of cells that were mCherry positive when gating such that ~1%
of cells transduced with a pre-crRNA array containing non-targeting control crRNAs are
mCherry positive (Fig. 4g, Supp. Fig 5). We find that ~4% of cells that received the
NGN3 targeting array are mCherry positive, while ~1.25% of cells that received the
“core” pre-crRNA array and ~3.5% of cells that received the “Core+Accessory”
pre-crRNA array are mCherry positive. As expected, activation of the accessory factors
alone did not lead to an increase in mCherry positive cells over control (Fig. 4h). While
we did not observe higher rates of mCherry positive cells in the Core or Core+Accessory
conditions vs. the NGN3-targeting array, we do observe an (~3x) increase in mCherry
positive cells between Core and Core+Accessory conditions, suggesting increased
differentiation efficiency due to multiplexed activation. Furthermore, we observe
increased (~2x) MFI of the mCherry positive population in the Core+Accessory condition
vs. both the NGN3 and core conditions, suggesting higher TUBB3A expression in these
cells (Fig. 4i).
Together, these results demonstrate that dCas12a activators are capable of multiplexed
activation of gene expression in multiple primary cell systems in which dCas12a
effectors have been integrated and remain stably expressed.
5. The inclusion of a control library with 10,000 non-targeting six-crRNA arrays and three pre-crRNAs
targeting the PER1 promoter seems excessive. The rationale for this large imbalance between
non-targeting and targeting arrays should be clarified. How does this control design contribute to the
study's objectives?
Since most of the targeting library is composed of pre-crRNA arrays targeting both enhancers, it
would be difficult to detect depletion from the high (top 12.5%) PER1 expression bin and enrichment
in the low (bottom 12.5%) PER1 expression bin if only a small fraction of the library was composed of
non-targeting pre-crRNA arrays. We included many non-targeting pre-crRNA arrays so that we could
detect whether the pre-crRNA arrays targeting both enhancers were well separated from negative
controls and conservatively designed our library to contain ~50% non-targeting pre-crRNAs arrays
and ~50% dual-targeting pre-crRNA arrays.
We have added text to the manuscript to justify this design choice on lines 648-652. It reads:
In parallel, we separately constructed a control library of 10,000 non-targeting six-crRNA
arrays and three pre-crRNAs targeting the PER1 promoter (Supp. Fig 13). Since most
(80%) of the PER1-targeting library consists of pre-crRNAs targeting both enhancers,
this large control library will enable better separation between cells with high and low
PER1 expression.
6. The diagrams in Fig. 7b-d are confusing. Are these plots representing PER1-high cells or
PER1-low cells? A more detailed explanation of how these plots were generated is necessary to help
understanding.
Thank you for this comment. We originally showed the average of the two bins, but have revised Fig.
8 (previously Fig. 7) to show the high and low bin separately since this is how we refer to the data in
the text.
7. The purpose of testing the two enhancers using a large library is unclear. The authors should
elaborate on why not use a few well-designed crRNA arrays to target individual or paired enhancers
and measure the downstream gene expression? It is unclear if there is a necessity of performing
library screening on two enhancers of one gene. Furthermore, the insights gained from testing PER1
enhancers can be strengthened.
Identifying interactions between gene regulatory elements remains a major challenge for numerous
technical, biological, and statistical reasons. Specifically, experimental noise, potentially weak
biological effects, and the compounding of those factors in statistical analyses typically leaves studies
of genetic interactions highly underpowered. Using rough estimates of how those factors would
impact the new dCas12a systems developed here, we developed a screen where we were highly
confident in our statistical power. Indeed, we feel that the depth of analysis in this screen can serve
as a starting point for more formal power analyses to guide future study designs.
To clarify that point to readers, we added the following text to the discussion on lines 813-816:
A key observation from our screen of the PER1 locus is that identifying epistatic
interactions in gene regulation requires a great degree of replication, and we
expect that the outcomes of our study can be useful for power analyses to design
future such screens.
8. The manuscript would benefit from discussing specific design rules for guide RNA arrays.
We believe that we address this concern throughout the manuscript. Specifically, we observed that
crRNAs towards the end of an array have low activity, but that this can be rescued by using an RNA
Pol II promoter. We do not observe clear evidence of positional effects in the PER1 enhancer screen.
We looked further into that screen data and did find crRNAs that, when included in the array, led to
significantly stronger or weaker repression. This data is shown in Supp. Fig. 17, and text describing
these results on lines 705-714 and is reproduced below:
We did not find strong evidence for substantial heterogeneity in the effects of the
individual crRNAs. Specifically, we tested if, when targeting enhancer A or B individually,
any of the crRNAs consistently increased or decreased the effect of the pre-crRNA array
(Supp. Table 3). In the 100 nM Dex high bin, 2 of the 9 crRNAs targeting enhancer A
had significant effects and 6 of the 9 crRNAs targeting enhancer B had a significant
effect (FDR < 0.05). Of those eight crRNAs with significant effects, four increased crRNA
array activity, and four decreased that activity. However, the magnitude of those effects
were small, with changes in mean pre-crRNA enrichment of between 10% and 36%
when those crRNAs were present (Supp. Fig 17a-c). The individual crRNA effects also
did not correlate with GC content or the on-target activity score predicted by CRISPick
(Supp. Table 3).
Since there are only 18 unique crRNAs in the screen, we feel that there is not sufficient data to
comment decisively about positioning or design rules.
9. Citations 73-74: The manuscript does not appropriately cite work on Cas13. The authors should
ensure they reference the most relevant studies.
Thank you for this comment, we now cite:
East-Seletsky, A., O’Connell, M., Knight, S. et al. Two distinct RNase activities of CRISPR-C2c2 enable
guide-RNA processing and RNA detection. Nature 538, 270–273 (2016).
https://doi.org/10.1038/nature19802
To substantiate our claim that Cas13a can process its own crRNA array.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors provided explanations and revisions to the manuscript reasonably addressed my comments. I have no further questions.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Thank you for the thoughtful revision. The manuscript is improved, and many of our earlier concerns are addressed in the text. That said, a few key issues remain around robustness in primary T cells. Most of the changes are textual rather than experimental, so the main uncertainty is still how well the system performs in a more complex, physiologically relevant setting.
Major points:
• Particularly, P300 is described as part of the toolkit but is not shown in primary T cells. Even a small pilot (e.g., n=2 donors) would help establish whether P300 is workable in this context. If those data aren’t feasible now, the authors should at least say so explicitly and acknowledge that P300 remains untested in primary T cells and reduce the claim of broad applicability.
• Not all target genes were repressed is a main issue for robustness. Primary cell experiments can be variable, but this highlights that the system isn't a simple "plug-and-play" tool. It requires target-specific optimization. The authors should clearly explain in the main text that its application in primary T cells appears more preliminary and would benefit from further optimization.
Minor points:
• In earlier rounds of reviews, we’ve requested the authors to add numerical P-values. The request for P-values was not for significance thresholds (indicated by asterisks), but for the exact numerical P-values.
• While the authors corrected most of the supplementary figure labeling inconsistencies (Supplementary Fig. xx), there is still one missed at line 424.
• The sentence on line 291 remains ambiguous. We suggest the authors consider: 'Although not all target genes showed measurable effects in this cell type, these findings demonstrate the potential of dCas12a for multiplexed repression in primary cells.’
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5: I co-reviewed this manuscript with one of the reviewers who provided the listed reports. This is part of the Nature Communications initiative to facilitate training in peer review and to provide appropriate recognition for Early Career Researchers who co-review manuscripts.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:

Reviewer #4 (Remarks to the Author):
Thank you for the thoughtful revision. The manuscript is improved, and many of our earlier concerns are

We also did not evaluate dCas12a-P300 fusions in primary T cells, and the efficacy of
